title: Om mani padme hum
hookLine: the six-syllable mantra of Avalokiteshvara, whom Tibetans call Chenrezig

cards: Stones with letters carved into them line the trails of the Tibetan Himalaya, sometimes painted, sometimes piled into long walls taller than a person.
On a bench in Dharamsala or Kathmandu, an old woman murmurs, beads slipping through her fingers, the same short sound again and again. Some people keep count on their beads from morning to night.
The stones and the woman are saying the same six syllables.

teach.b: Om mani padme hum. In Tibetan it's usually om mani peme hung. It's the mantra of Avalokiteshvara, whom you met in the Heart Sutra, looking deep.
Tibetans call him Chenrezig, the one who looks with eyes of compassion, and Tibetan tradition regards the Dalai Lama as his emanation.

The mantra appears in an Indian Mahayana text, the Karandavyuha Sutra, and traveled to Tibet with the teachers. What does it mean? Om is a sacred syllable Buddhism shares with older Indian traditions.
Mani means jewel. Padme has to do with the lotus. Hum is a seed syllable with no dictionary meaning.
So the familiar English reading is the jewel in the lotus.
That phrase became popular through European scholars, and some scholars read the grammar differently, perhaps as a call: O jewel-lotus one. Nobody can settle it for certain.
Tibetan teachers tend to explain it by what it does. The jewel is the wish to help others. The lotus, which grows clean out of mud, is wisdom.
Together they're the whole path: compassion and wisdom joined. Some teachers also link the six syllables to the six realms of rebirth, each syllable easing the suffering of one. And the stones?

Carving the mantra, or paying someone to carve it, is an act of merit, and the stones sit where travelers pass, kept on their right as they walk. The mantra is so short that anyone can carry it. That's much of the point.

how: Tibetan Buddhists recite Om mani padme hum aloud or under their breath through the day, often counting on a string of 108 beads, and carve or paint it on stones placed along paths and on walls that walkers pass on their right-hand side.

games.q: you're walking a Himalayan path and come to a long wall of carved mani stones. how do Tibetans usually pass it?
games.why: walkers keep the stones on their right, circling clockwise, the way one walks around a stupa.

practice: If you'd like, say om mani padme hum softly twenty-one times, counting on your fingers or on beads if you have them, more a murmur than a chant.
If saying it doesn't feel right for you, listen to it inwardly, or just count twenty-one breaths. When you finish, let the sound fade and sit in what's left.

wordCard.voice: Chenrezig. The bodhisattva of compassion, called Avalokiteshvara in Sanskrit, whose six-syllable mantra is om mani padme hum.

orig.note: Sanskrit: om (sacred syllable), maṇi (jewel), padme (lotus), hūṃ (seed syllable). Tibetans often say om mani peme hung.
